players.product: leading-edge wafer fab (N3/N2 GAA logic dies)

quarterly_data.signal: Q3 2026 results (CFO Wendell Huang): revenue increased 17.6% sequentially in NT; in U.S. dollar terms revenue increased 16.2% sequentially to $46.7 billion, above the high end of the third-quarter guidance, supported by strong demand for leading-edge process technologies. Gross margin decreased 1.3 percentage points sequentially to 66.4%, primarily due to margin dilution from the 2 nm ramp; total operating expenses 7.8% of net revenue; operating margin 58.7%; EPS TWD 29.43; ROE 45.5%. Wafer revenue by node: 2 nm 8%, 3 nm 33%, 5 nm 28%, 7 nm 10%; advanced technologies (7 nm and below) 79%. By platform: HPC increased 22% quarter-over-quarter to 68% of revenue; smartphone increased 10% to 21%; IoT increased 5% to 4%; automotive increased 23% to 4%; DCE declined 12% to 1%. Cash and marketable securities TWD 4 trillion, or $126 billion; about TWD 920 billion cash from operations in the quarter.
quarterly_data.figure: Q3 revenue $46.7 billion (+16.2% sequentially in U.S. dollar terms); gross margin 66.4%; operating margin 58.7%; 2 nm 8% of wafer revenue; HPC 68% of revenue

quarterly_data.signal: Guidance (CFO): Q4 2026 revenue between $52.3 billion and $54.3 billion, a 14% sequential increase or a 58% year-over-year increase at the midpoint; at an exchange rate assumption of one U.S. dollar to TWD 31.8, gross margin between 65% and 67% and operating margin between 56.5% and 58.5%. Q4 gross margin is guided to decrease 40 basis points to 66% at the midpoint, primarily due to continued dilution from the steep ramp-up of 2 nm and dilution from overseas fabs, partially offset by cost improvement efforts (productivity gains, across node capacity optimization). Full year: CEO C.C. Wei now expects 2026 revenue growth of around 44% year-over-year in U.S. dollar terms, as demand for leading-edge technologies continues to be 'extremely robust'. He added that consumer and price-sensitive end market segments are being challenged by rising component prices and macroeconomic uncertainties, so TSMC is 'being prudent in our business planning going into 2027'.
quarterly_data.figure: Q4 2026 revenue between $52.3 billion and $54.3 billion; gross margin between 65% and 67%; operating margin between 56.5% and 58.5%; FY2026 revenue growth around 44% in U.S. dollar terms

quarterly_data.signal: Profitability view: the CFO said that, thanks to the company's larger scale and cost improvement efforts, TSMC now expects the gross margin dilution from the ramp-up of its overseas fabs to be closer to 2% (wording garbled in the transcript), but with more fabs ramping in the U.S. the overseas dilution is expected to widen to 3%-4% in the next few years; in Q&A he confirmed 3 to 4 percentage points in the second part of the five-year period 'still remain the case', as TSMC is 'accelerating everywhere, including in the U.S.' TSMC will leverage its increasing size in Arizona to improve the cost structure and says it remains the most cost-efficient manufacturer in every region where it operates. CEO C.C. Wei on long-term margins: 'there is no ceiling for TSMC's profitability, but a dramatic increase will not happen overnight either.' On pricing, he said the strategy is 'very strategic' and depends on market segment, location and technology; production in the U.S. will be priced 'a little bit different from the one we produce in Taiwan', and TSMC tries 'to get our value to be recognized'.
quarterly_data.figure: overseas-fab gross margin dilution closer to 2%, widening to 3%-4% in the next few years

quarterly_data.signal: Capex (CFO): Q3 2026 capital expenditures totaled $13.8 billion (TWD 443 billion). Given continued robust multi-year customer demand, including the emerging agentic AI market, TSMC reiterated its full year 2026 capital budget at between $60 billion and $64 billion, and still expects 2026 to 2028 capex to be significantly higher than the past three years. Tool supply is tight, so TSMC collaborates with its tool suppliers well in advance to prepare capacity; 'the tool price inflation is real' (tool price, material, labor cost), but the majority of capex relates to long-term demand. It is too early to give a capex number beyond this year; on capital intensity, 'the increase in revenue will outpace the increase in CapEx, and that is still the case'. CEO C.C. Wei on High NA EUV: 'our plan is to use it in 2030', when it is mature and its cost reasonable, and TSMC is working closely with ASML to establish a 12 in photomask by 2031; using it later than competitors is not a disadvantage, he said, because TSMC remains 'the best company to offer the most advanced technology'.
quarterly_data.figure: Q3 capex $13.8 billion (TWD 443 billion); 2026 capital budget between $60 billion and $64 billion (reiterated); High NA EUV use planned in 2030

quarterly_data.signal: Supply vs demand (CEO C.C. Wei): after weighing CSP capex, data-center build-out, financial, power supply and other component supply, 'we still think the demand is higher than the supply, and we are working very hard to narrow the gap'; 'the gap between demand and supply are still quite big', and whether it widens next year he said 'I cannot answer this question right now because of my customer continue to increase their demand'. TSMC now sends its own teams to check data-center build-out progress and the power supply situation in the U.S.: 'so far so good, and the CSPs has been well-prepared'. CFO: too early to give a capacity-growth percentage; the increase in advanced nodes is the main driver of capacity increase. On a secondary wafer market, the CEO said TSMC does not allow customers to sublet or auction off capacity; in certain cases customers collaborate through a mask licensing agreement, and 'the amount is very, very small'.

Node roadmap (CEO C.C. Wei): TSMC is expanding at an unprecedented pace with nearly 20 fabs worldwide in progress: 13 leading-edge and advanced packaging fabs in Taiwan over the next several years and another five to six fabs overseas. N2 entered high-volume manufacturing in the fourth quarter of 2025 with good yield and is ramping in multiple phases at both Hsinchu and Kaohsiung; N2 family annual capacity is expected to more than double in 2027 on smartphone and HPC AI demand. TSMC has begun preparing A14 capacity: risk production on track for 2027, volume production to start in 2028; A14 is seeing more customers than the 2 nm activities so far and is expected to be a bigger node than N2. Asked about an IDM customer, he said TSMC treats IDM and fabless customers the same, takes customers' internal capacity into consideration and does not comment on a specific customer. Running smartphone small dies and AI accelerator big dies on a new node at the same time is 'to TSMC's advantage'; backside power (Super Power Rail) adoption depends on the customer's product, with some accelerators possibly using it and mobile phones not.
quarterly_data.figure: nearly 20 fabs worldwide in progress; N2 family annual capacity to more than double in 2027; A14 risk production 2027, volume production 2028

quarterly_data.signal: N3 capacity and overseas fabs (CEO C.C. Wei): TSMC is executing a global plan of three new fabs for 3 nm. Taiwan: volume production at the new 3 nm fab in Tainan Science Park on track to begin in the first half of 2027, and driven by strong customer demand TSMC has decided to add one additional 3 nm fab in Tainan, with volume production scheduled for the first half of 2028. Arizona: construction of the second fab is complete and tool move-in and installation is under way; volume production will begin in third quarter 2027, slightly ahead of the previous schedule. Japan: plan to use 3 nm in the second fab, volume production scheduled in 2028. TSMC continues to convert 5 nm tools to support 3 nm capacity in Taiwan and to run flexible capacity support among N7, N5 and N3. U.S. expansion: most of TSMC's large customers are in the U.S. and request more U.S. capacity, and the U.S. government is 'very helpful'; TSMC is evaluating sites outside Arizona, Texas being one, and has sent teams there; it is also discussing with one customer that is building a fab, Terafab, whether TSMC can utilize that capacity, still in discussion, and 'the fab has to be run by TSMC'. 'We have no intention to leave food on the table for others.'
quarterly_data.figure: additional 3 nm fab in Tainan, volume production first half of 2028; Arizona second fab volume production third quarter 2027; Japan second fab 3 nm volume production 2028

players.product: N3/N2-class processed logic wafers (Rubin GPU + Vera CPU dies)

quarterly_data.signal: AI demand (CEO C.C. Wei): the AI market 'continues to be very strong'; increasing AI demand is fueled by rising adoption of agentic AI as the industry moves from chatbots to AI assistance, and greater adoption of open source AI models should lower the barrier to AI usage and drive more demand for leading-edge silicon. The emergence of agentic AI CPUs and continued demand for networking chips drive further silicon demand, and 'all the AI players are working with TSMC'. On the AI accelerator revenue CAGR that TSMC had guided at mid to high 50s percentage for 2024 to 2029 (IR head Jeff Su), the CEO said 'We did not see any sign of slowdown. Whether it is a high 50 CAGR, it does not matter. It probably will be higher.' Demand from agentic AI CPUs continues to increase, but CPUs stay outside the narrow AI accelerator definition because TSMC cannot identify conventional versus AI server CPU use (Jeff Su: 'it is certainly part of our business'). In TSMC's judgment AI demand 'is still far above our capability today to supply'.
quarterly_data.figure: AI accelerator CAGR (mid to high 50s percentage, 2024 to 2029) 'probably will be higher'

quarterly_data.signal: Advanced packaging (CEO C.C. Wei): TSMC is in real-world production of 5x reticle size packaging - 'I don't believe that anybody can do that today except at TSMC, and the yield is excellent' - and is working on 9x reticle size and moving into 14x reticle size, while working on CoWoS to offer a reasonable cost reduction. 'The CoWoS is still the number one choice for our customer', though a competitor offers 'a very competitive solution'. Asked whether TSMC would back up customers if a competitor's packaging (EMIB-T) cannot deliver, he said 'yes, we will be', since the number one priority is that customers' products are introduced into the market smoothly.
quarterly_data.figure: 5x reticle size in production; 9x and 14x reticle size in development

quarterly_data.signal: Back-end supply partner: asked about the recent TSMC announcement with GlobalFoundries on interposers (as IR head Jeff Su put it), CEO C.C. Wei said the GlobalFoundries deal 'is part of our overall strategy in the back-end supply': 'Definitely, we have a little bit shortage on the back end', and TSMC will work with partner GlobalFoundries so that both companies can support TSMC's customers with enough capacity.
